templates.title: Authorization-to-capture funnel
templates.subtopic: pre-aggregation before joins, cohort attribution, ratios

sections.scenario: Card payments on a payments platform can be authorized first and captured later: the authorization places a hold on the customer's card, the capture moves the money, and a void releases the hold without capturing. Merchants that ship goods before capturing want a daily funnel: of what we authorized, how much did we actually capture, and how much did we void? Amounts are stored as integers in the currency's smallest unit (cents for usd, whole yen for jpy).
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every (auth_date, merchant_id, currency) with at least {{min_auths}} authorizations: auth_date (the UTC date of authorized_at), merchant_id, currency, authorizations (count), voided (authorizations with a void), captured_auths (authorizations with at least one successful capture), authorized_amount, captured_amount (sum of successful captures), capture_rate_count = ROUND(captured_auths / authorizations, 4) and capture_rate_amount = ROUND(captured_amount / authorized_amount, 4), both computed in numeric. Order by auth_date, merchant_id, currency. {{capture_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Never add amounts across currencies: each currency is its own row. The sample has {{n_auths}} authorizations; production has millions per day across many merchants.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, merchants and amounts. All amounts are integers in minor units and a capture is in its authorization's currency. A void and a successful capture never happen to the same authorization. Authorizations that are neither captured nor voided are still pending and stay in the denominator.
sections.criteria: Aggregates captures per authorization before joining (no fan-out); successful captures only; attributes captures to the authorization's day; keeps voids in the denominator; one row per currency; numeric division with ROUND to 4; inclusive minimum; deterministic ordering.

clarifications.q: Which day does a capture belong to?
clarifications.a: The day of its authorization. The funnel is a cohort of authorizations, so a capture that lands the next day still counts toward the day the authorization was made.

clarifications.q: Do voided authorizations count in the denominator?
clarifications.a: Yes. A void is one outcome of an authorization; it stays in authorizations and authorized_amount.

clarifications.q: If one authorization is captured in three parts, how many captured authorizations is that?
clarifications.a: One. captured_amount adds all three parts.

clarifications.q: Should I convert currencies to compare merchants?
clarifications.a: No. There is no exchange-rate table; report each currency on its own row.

clarifications.q: Is the minimum inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A group with exactly {{min_auths}} authorizations is reported.

hints: Reduce captures to one row per authorization first (successful captures only), then join that to authorizations. Joining raw capture rows repeats the authorization.
COUNT(x) counts non-null values, so a LEFT JOIN plus COUNT(captured_amount) counts captured authorizations directly.
Cast before dividing: count::numeric / count. Integer division truncates.
followups: The same report at billions of authorizations: which table do you pre-aggregate, at what grain, and how does it stay correct when a capture arrives days later?
Finance wants one company-wide capture rate across all currencies. What would you need, and what would you refuse to do?
Uncaptured authorizations expire after a period set by the card network. How would you add an "expired" bucket to the funnel without a status column?
Some captures exceed the authorized amount for certain payment methods and merchant categories. Which parts of this query assume they never do, and what would you change?

rules.ask: If one authorization has three partial captures, how many rows does your join produce, and what does that do to authorizations and authorized_amount?
A capture lands the day after its authorization. Which day's row should it change, and why is the funnel a cohort?
Two currencies in one SUM: what number did you just produce, and who would be misled by it?
Which of your counts would change if a capture row were duplicated by an upstream retry?

templates.title: The refund that crossed the cap
templates.subtopic: running sums, frames and deterministic tie-breaks

sections.scenario: A charge can be refunded in several partial refunds, but the total refunded may never exceed what was captured. An API enforces that limit when a refund is created; the warehouse copy of the data is used to audit it. A risk analyst asks: which charges ended up refunded beyond their cap, and which refund pushed each one over?
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns one row per charge whose cumulative counted refunds exceed its cap: charge_id, merchant_id, breach_refund_id (the first refund, in time order, after which the running total is greater than the cap), breached_at (that refund's created_at), refunded_total (the running total after that refund), amount_captured and excess = refunded_total − amount_captured. Order by breached_at, charge_id. {{status_rule}} {{cap_rule}} {{tie_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Strictly greater: a charge refunded to exactly its captured amount is fully refunded, not over. Report only the first breaching refund per charge. The sample has {{n_refunds}} refunds.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema and amounts, all integers in minor units in the charge's currency. The audit data deliberately contains breaches the API would have refused, so the query has something to find.
sections.criteria: Running sum per charge with a fully specified order and ROWS frame; status filter before the window; cap is amount_captured; strict comparison; exactly one row per breaching charge; deterministic ordering; can explain how the API should prevent the race the audit detects.

clarifications.q: Do later refunds that are also over the cap get rows?
clarifications.a: No. One row per charge: the first refund that took the running total over the cap.

clarifications.q: What is the cap?
clarifications.a: amount_captured. For a partially captured charge that is less than amount.

clarifications.q: Which refunds count?
clarifications.a: Only refunds that moved or committed money: failed and canceled refunds are excluded before you compute the running total.

clarifications.q: What if two refunds on one charge have the same created_at?
clarifications.a: Order by created_at, then refund_id. The result must be deterministic.

clarifications.q: Is a running total equal to the cap a breach?
clarifications.a: No. Only strictly greater.

hints: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY charge_id ORDER BY created_at, refund_id) gives the running total after each refund.
Filter out failed refunds before the window function, not after: a filtered-out row must not contribute to anyone's running total.
Then keep the rows over the cap and take the first per charge (ROW_NUMBER() or DISTINCT ON).
followups: Your window has ORDER BY created_at only. What does the default frame do with two refunds at the same second, and how does the answer change?
The API must refuse a refund that would cross the cap, under concurrent requests for the same charge. What does it need: a lock, a conditional update, a ledger? Sketch it.
Disputes can also take money back from a charge. How would you extend the cap check so refunds and dispute losses together never exceed the captured amount?
The refunds table has billions of rows. How do you make this audit incremental, so a nightly run touches only charges with new refunds?

rules.ask: Two refunds on one charge share a created_at. What running total does each get under your frame, and which refund do you report?
Did your status filter run before or after the window function, and what would the other order compute?
Which column is the cap for a charge that was captured only in part?
What is the cost of your approach on a charge with 500 small refunds, compared with a single running-sum window?

templates.title: Webhook endpoints that keep failing

sections.scenario: A payments platform notifies merchants of events (a payment succeeded, a refund was issued, an invoice was paid) by sending HTTPS POST requests to the webhook endpoints they register. A delivery succeeds when the endpoint answers with a 2xx status; otherwise it is retried for a while. Support wants to contact merchants whose endpoints are in trouble: an endpoint that fails many events in a row is more urgent than one with scattered failures.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every endpoint whose longest run of consecutive failed events is at least {{min_streak}}: endpoint_id, events (events for that endpoint), delivered_events (events with at least one 2xx attempt), avg_first_success_s (average seconds from created_at to the first 2xx attempt, over delivered events, ROUND(…, 1)), longest_failure_streak, and streak_started_at (the created_at of the first event in that run; if two runs tie, the earlier run). An event has failed if it was never delivered. Events are ordered per endpoint by created_at, event_id. Order the result by longest_failure_streak DESC, endpoint_id. {{attempt_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A success is a status code from 200 to 299 inclusive. The sample has {{n_events}} events.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical endpoints, event types, retry timings and status codes. Each webhook_events row is one event for one endpoint. The retry window has closed for every event in the sample, so "never delivered" is final.
sections.criteria: Event-level outcomes from attempts (any 2xx, first success); LEFT JOIN keeps unattempted events; consecutive runs via gaps and islands with a deterministic order; earliest longest run; latency over delivered events only; inclusive threshold; deterministic result ordering.

clarifications.q: Is a streak about attempts or events?
clarifications.a: Events. An event that failed twice and then succeeded is a delivered event and breaks a streak.

clarifications.q: Does a redirect count as delivered?
clarifications.a: No. Only 2xx counts; redirects are not followed.

clarifications.q: What about an event with no attempts at all?
clarifications.a: It was never delivered, so it is a failed event and belongs in the streak.

clarifications.q: Latency to which success, if there are several?
clarifications.a: The first 2xx attempt. A later re-send does not change when the event was first delivered.

clarifications.q: Is the threshold inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A run of exactly {{min_streak}} qualifies.

hints: Reduce attempts to one row per event first: MIN(attempted_at) FILTER (WHERE status_code BETWEEN 200 AND 299), from a LEFT JOIN so events with no attempts survive.
Gaps and islands: ROW_NUMBER() over all events minus ROW_NUMBER() within the failed events is constant along each run of consecutive failures.
Pick each endpoint's longest run with DISTINCT ON (endpoint_id) … ORDER BY endpoint_id, len DESC, start.
followups: The same report every five minutes over a stream of attempts. What state do you keep per endpoint so you never rescan history?
Retries back off over hours. When is an event's outcome final, and how do you report an endpoint that is failing right now, before its events are final?
Support now wants to automatically disable endpoints that fail too much. What signal would you use, and how do you avoid disabling a merchant for one bad deploy?
How would you tell an endpoint that is down from one that is slow (timeouts) from one that rejects a single event type?

rules.ask: An endpoint fails 10 events, but never 3 in a row. Does your query flag it, and should it?
An event the platform never managed to attempt has no rows in delivery_attempts. Where does it go in your query?
Which codes count as success in your query, and what happens to a 204, a 302 and a timeout with no status?
How do you get the length and start of each run from LAG alone, and what does that cost compared with the row-number difference?

templates.title: Idempotency keys with a 24-hour memory

sections.scenario: Payment APIs let a client send an idempotency key with a POST request so a retry after a network error cannot charge a customer twice. Public API documentation describes the shape: the first request with a key is executed and its result saved; a later request with the same key gets the saved result back; reusing a key with different parameters is an error; and keys can be forgotten after 24 hours. You are writing the decision logic for a replay of the request log.
sections.problem: Implement idempotency_outcomes(requests, max_keys=None). requests is a list of (ts_seconds, key, params_hash) sorted by ts_seconds. Return one string per request: "execute" if the key is not live (first use, or its previous life has expired), "replay" if the key is live and params_hash equals the one stored at first use, or "conflict" if the key is live and the parameters differ. A key executed at time t is live while ts < t + 86400; at exactly t + 86400 it has expired and behaves as new. Replays and conflicts never extend a key's life or change its stored parameters. {{tie_rule}} {{cap_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 requests; keys and hashes are short strings; timestamps are non-decreasing integers. Expected: O(1) amortised work per request and memory proportional to the live keys.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical traffic. Real APIs also scope keys to an account and store the full response; here the store records only the first-use time and the parameters hash.
sections.criteria: Correct half-open 24-hour life; replays and conflicts do not extend it; expired keys behave as new; amortised O(1) with a justification (queue in first-use order); at the Very Hard level, purges expired keys before applying the cap and evicts the oldest live key. Discusses concurrency and in-flight requests honestly.

clarifications.q: Is a request exactly 24 hours after first use a replay?
clarifications.a: No. At exactly 86 400 seconds the key has expired; that request executes and starts a new 24-hour life.

clarifications.q: Does a replay refresh the 24 hours?
clarifications.a: No. Expiry is measured from first use only.

clarifications.q: After a conflict, which parameters are stored?
clarifications.a: Still the first request's. A conflict changes nothing.

clarifications.q: Can an expired key come back with different parameters?
clarifications.a: Yes. It behaves as a brand-new key and executes.

hints: A dict from key to (first_ts, params_hash) answers live lookups in O(1).
Keys expire in the same order they were first used, because timestamps never go backwards. A FIFO queue of (first_ts, key) lets you drop expired keys from the front before each request.
Each key enters the queue once per life and leaves once, which is where amortised O(1) comes from.
followups: The store now runs on 30 API servers behind a load balancer. Two retries with the same key arrive at two servers within a millisecond. What makes exactly one of them execute?
The first request is still running when its retry arrives. What should the retry get back, and what must the store record while the first request is in flight?
Memory: 50 000 requests per second, each with a key, kept for 24 hours. Estimate the store's size and say how you would bound it.
The process crashes after charging the card but before saving the result. What does the retry see, and how would you design the write order so this cannot double-charge?

rules.ask: The store is unavailable for 30 seconds. Do you reject requests that carry idempotency keys, or execute them without protection, and why?
Your store's TTL deletes keys lazily. Which requests near the 24-hour boundary could get a different answer from the one specified?
How many keys are live at once in the timing test, and what does a per-request scan cost?
What happens to a key whose holder dies while holding the lock?

templates.title: Card testing across merchants

sections.scenario: Card testing is a fraud pattern in which someone with stolen card numbers makes many small attempts to find out which cards work. One signal is velocity: the same card (identified by a fingerprint, not the raw number) attempting payments at many different merchants in a short time, which honest cardholders rarely do. You are writing the batch job that finds the moment each card first crossed a velocity threshold.
sections.problem: Implement first_flags(events, k, window_s, declined_only=False). events is a list of (ts, card_fingerprint, merchant_id, outcome) sorted by ts, with outcome either 'approved' or 'declined'. Return a dict from card fingerprint to the first timestamp t at which that card's counted attempts with timestamps in the closed window [t − window_s, t] span at least k distinct merchants. Cards that never reach it are absent. {{count_rule}} {{tie_rule}} In the samples, k = {{k}} and window_s = {{window_s}}.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 events; a card can have thousands of attempts inside one window. Expected: O(1) amortised work per event.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical thresholds and traffic. A real system combines many signals; this one is deliberately simple.
sections.criteria: Closed window; distinct merchants via counts, not a set; per-card state; first timestamp only; declined-only filter applied before counting; amortised O(1) with a justification; sensible discussion of partitioning and out-of-order events.

clarifications.q: Is an attempt exactly window_s seconds earlier inside the window?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window is closed: [t − window_s, t].

clarifications.q: Do two attempts at the same merchant count twice?
clarifications.a: No. Distinct merchants.

clarifications.q: Once a card is flagged, do I keep reporting it?
clarifications.a: No. Only the first timestamp. You can stop tracking that card.

clarifications.q: When declined_only is True, do approved attempts affect anything?
clarifications.a: No. They are ignored entirely.

hints: Per card, keep a queue of its counted attempts in the window and a dict from merchant to how many of those attempts were at that merchant.
When an attempt leaves the window, decrement its merchant's count and delete the merchant only when the count reaches zero. A plain set loses a merchant that still has a later attempt inside.
The number of distinct merchants is the size of that dict, so checking the threshold is O(1).
followups: The same detection on a live stream across 40 consumers. How do you partition the events, and what goes wrong if you partition by merchant?
Events arrive up to 2 minutes out of order. How would you change the window logic, and what does that do to the "first timestamp"?
A fraud ring rotates through thousands of card numbers at one merchant instead. Which other key would you count distinct values for, and how does your state grow?
Memory is bounded per card by the window. What happens with 100 million active cards, and what approximate structure would you accept?

rules.ask: A card used merchant A at second 0 and again at second 50, with a 100-second window. At second 101 is A still counted in your structure?
Card testing spreads across merchants. Which consumer sees all of one card's attempts under your partitioning?
What is the cost per event when a card has 3 000 attempts inside the window?
What false-positive or undercount rate would you accept for blocking a card, and who pays for each kind of error?

templates.title: Best currency conversion within K conversions

sections.scenario: A treasury team moves a merchant's balance between currencies before a payout. Liquidity providers publish quotes: convert from one currency to another at a rate, minus a fee in basis points. Every extra conversion adds settlement risk and operational work, so treasury allows at most a fixed number of conversions per route. You are writing the routine that finds the best route for a given amount over a snapshot of quotes.
sections.problem: Implement best_conversion(quotes, source, target, amount, max_hops). Each quote is (from_ccy, to_ccy, rate_micros, fee_bps). Converting x minor units along one quote yields x * rate_micros * (10000 - fee_bps) // 10_000_000_000 minor units of to_ccy: the integer result is floored after every conversion, never once at the end. Return the largest amount of target obtainable from amount minor units of source using at most max_hops conversions, or None if no route of at most max_hops conversions reaches target. With zero conversions, source itself holds amount. {{fee_rule}} {{hop_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 400 currencies and 25 000 quotes; 0 ≤ max_hops ≤ 8; amounts up to 10⁹ minor units. Use integer arithmetic only. O(max_hops · number of quotes) time is expected.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical quotes and fees. rate_micros is the rate times 10⁶ and already accounts for each currency's minor unit (zero-decimal currencies such as JPY have no cents), so the formula above is all you need. A quote is directional: a quote from A to B says nothing about B to A.
sections.criteria: Integer arithmetic with a floor after every hop; at-most semantics with a copy per step; distinguishes 0 from unreachable; handles parallel quotes and revisits; O(K·E) with a justification from monotonicity; explains why quote loops need the hop limit.

clarifications.q: Is a route with fewer than max_hops conversions allowed?
clarifications.a: Yes. At most max_hops; 0 conversions is allowed when source equals target.

clarifications.q: Can a route pass through the same currency twice?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each conversion counts toward max_hops.

clarifications.q: What do I return if the best reachable amount floors to 0?
clarifications.a: 0. None means the target is unreachable within max_hops, which is a different answer.

clarifications.q: Can there be two quotes for the same pair?
clarifications.a: Yes, from different providers with different rates and fees. Consider each.

clarifications.q: May I use floats for the rate?
clarifications.a: No. Money stays in integer minor units, and the floor after every hop is part of the specification.

hints: Let best_i[c] be the most of currency c you can hold after at most i conversions. best_0 has only source.
Each conversion is monotone: more in means at least as much out. That is why keeping only the best amount per currency per step is safe.
Compute step i + 1 from a copy of step i. Relaxing quotes in place can chain several conversions inside one step and exceed max_hops.
followups: Quotes expire every few seconds. How would you recompute the best routes for many (source, target, amount) requests without starting from scratch each time?
Fees in reality include a fixed part per conversion as well as basis points. Does your dynamic programme still work, and why?
A provider's quote has a minimum and maximum size. How does that change the algorithm, and is it still optimal to keep one best amount per currency?
Without a hop limit, a loop of quotes that gains value makes the answer unbounded. How would you detect such a loop in a quote snapshot, and what should the system do about it?

rules.ask: Your approach turns rates into floats or logs. Show a case where the floored integer answer differs, and how you would keep the result exact.
Dijkstra needs edge weights that never make a path better. Is that true here with quote loops and a hop limit?
If you relax quotes in place, how many conversions can one step chain? Walk through a three-quote chain with max_hops = 2.
How many routes are there with 400 currencies and 6 hops, and what does that mean for your running time?

templates.title: Linked-account groups from shared identifiers
templates.subtopic: union-find with path compression, risk signals

sections.scenario: A risk team reviews connected merchant accounts. Accounts that share a card fingerprint, a device id or a bank account may be run by the same people, and a large connected group is worth a human look. The team gets a daily extract of (account_id, kind, value) rows and wants the sizes of the connected groups so it can prioritise review.
sections.problem: Implement linked_groups(links, min_size, max_share=None). links is a list of (account_id, kind, value). Two accounts are directly linked when they share the same identifier, meaning the same (kind, value) pair. Linking is transitive: if A shares an identifier with B and B with C, all three are one group. Every account that appears in links belongs to exactly one group (possibly of size 1). Return the sizes of all groups with at least min_size accounts, largest first. {{kind_rule}} {{share_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 300 000 link rows and 150 000 accounts; rows may repeat. Near-linear time is expected.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical accounts and identifiers. A group is a signal for review, not a finding about anyone; the output is sizes only.
sections.criteria: Identifier keyed by (kind, value); distinct accounts; transitive groups including singletons; inclusive min_size; correct max_share by distinct holders; union-find with compression and union by size or an equivalent near-linear traversal; avoids pairwise linking; discusses incremental and distributed versions honestly.

clarifications.q: Do a card value and a device value that happen to be the same string link two accounts?
clarifications.a: No. An identifier is the (kind, value) pair.

clarifications.q: If a row appears twice, does it count twice?
clarifications.a: No. Group sizes count distinct accounts.

clarifications.q: Should accounts with no shared identifier appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, as groups of size 1, if min_size allows.

clarifications.q: Is min_size inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A group of exactly min_size accounts is reported.

clarifications.q: Does the output need account ids?
clarifications.a: No. Sizes only, sorted descending.

hints: You do not need an edge between every pair of accounts that share an identifier. Linking each holder to the first holder you saw is enough.
Union-find with path compression (or path halving) and union by size keeps each operation almost constant.
If identifiers can be ignored for being too common, you need their distinct-holder counts before you link anything.
followups: The extract arrives daily. How do you maintain the groups incrementally as new links appear, and what is hard about links that disappear?
One identifier links 40 000 accounts. Is that a ring or noise, and how would you decide the threshold for ignoring an identifier?
How would you compute this in Spark or SQL over billions of rows, where you cannot hold a union-find in one process?
The review team wants to know why two accounts are in one group. What would you store so that you can show the chain of shared identifiers?

rules.ask: An identifier shared by 5 000 accounts produces how many pairs? What does that do to your running time?
A traversal works. What does union-find give you that a traversal does not when links arrive one batch at a time?
What happens to a recursive find on a chain of 150 000 accounts in CPython, and how do you avoid it?
How many iterations does label propagation need on a long chain, and how would you bound them?

templates.title: Debug a payment-status webhook processor
templates.subtopic: idempotency, ordering, integer money, error handling

sections.scenario: A merchant's backend keeps its own copy of payment state, updated from webhook events sent by its payment provider. Public webhook documentation from payment providers warns that an event can be delivered more than once and that delivery order is not guaranteed, so the handler must be idempotent and must not trust arrival order. Finance reports that some refunds never appear, some payments show "processing" long after they succeeded, and a few fully refunded payments are shown as partly refunded. The handler below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix process_events(events) so that it meets this specification. events is a list of dicts in delivery order: {"id", "type", "payment", "amount"} plus "seq" on status events. {{delivery_rule}}

  1. Duplicates. An event whose id was already processed is acknowledged again and changes nothing.
  2. Status events (payment.processing, payment.succeeded, payment.failed) create the payment record on first sight, with that event's amount. A status event is applied only if its seq is greater than the seq of the status currently stored; an older one is acknowledged and ignored.
  3. Refunds (refund.succeeded) add amount (integer minor units) to the payment's refunded total. A refund for a payment that has no record yet cannot be applied: it is not acknowledged, goes to retry, and is not treated as processed, so a later redelivery is applied.
  4. Output. {"payments": {payment_id: {"status", "amount", "amount_refunded", "fully_refunded", "applied"}}, "acked": [...], "retry": [...]}. amount_refunded is an integer in minor units; fully_refunded is amount_refunded == amount; applied lists, in order, the ids of the events that changed that payment; acked and retry list delivery ids in delivery order.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 deliveries; linear time.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical event types and amounts, simplified from what public webhook documentation describes. seq increases with every status change at the source. Unknown event types do not occur in this exercise.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom; deduplicates by event id; orders by seq, not arrival; keeps money in integer minor units; never acknowledges an event that was not applied, and does not mark it seen; removes the shared mutable default; keeps the fix minimal and linear; adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is a redelivered event acknowledged?
clarifications.a: Yes. Acknowledge it again so the sender stops retrying, but apply nothing.

clarifications.q: What does acknowledging mean here?
clarifications.a: Its id goes into acked, which stands for answering the webhook with a success status. retry stands for answering with an error so the sender tries again later.

clarifications.q: Does a stale status event count as processed?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is acknowledged and marked seen, but it does not change the payment and is not in applied.

clarifications.q: Can a refund exceed the amount?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; do not add validation for it.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The tests point at each one.

hints: Read the deduplication key carefully: what identifies one delivery, and what identifies one change?
Print 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 and int(0.29 * 100) in Python.
Look at every place an exception could be swallowed, and at what gets acknowledged or marked seen before you know the event was applied.
Call _new_record twice and compare the two applied lists with is.
followups: Your process crashes after applying an event but before acknowledging it. What happens on redelivery, and what makes that safe?
The seen-set lives in memory. How do you persist it, how long do you keep each id, and what does that window have to do with the sender's retry schedule?
Instead of trusting the event payload, some teams fetch the current object from the provider's API when an event arrives. When is that better, and what does it cost?
A refund in retry never gets a matching payment event. How do you find out, and who should?

rules.ask: Two workers receive two events for the same payment at the same moment. Where exactly do you serialise, and what is the key?
Two status events for one payment share the same created second. What breaks ties, and why does this exercise use seq instead?
Decimal fixes the arithmetic. Why do payment systems still prefer integer minor units end to end?
How many times will the sender retry, over what period, and what do you do when the retries run out?

templates.title: Change data capture from the payments database to the lakehouse
templates.subtopic: CDC, snapshot handoff, ordering, schema evolution, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A payments platform runs its transactional database as {{shards}} relational shards: charges, refunds, disputes, balance transactions (each with amount, fee and net in integer minor units) and payouts. Analytics, finance and risk teams query a lakehouse copy of these tables. Today a nightly full export feeds the lakehouse; it takes longer every month and finance cannot close the books from data that is a day old. You are asked to replace it with change data capture at about {{change_rate}} at peak, with lakehouse tables no more than {{freshness}} behind.
sections.problem: Design CDC from the OLTP shards into the lakehouse with ledger-grade correctness: no lost row, no duplicated row and no row in the wrong version. Cover the initial snapshot of the largest table ({{largest_table}}) and its handoff to the stream, ordering and the log position you trust, updates and deletes, schema changes made by product teams, how tables are laid out and merged in the lakehouse, and the reconciliation that proves the copy is complete.
sections.constraints: The shards are production databases: the snapshot must not lock tables or hurt payment latency. The database keeps its change log for {{log_retention}}. Balance-transaction rows are append-only at the source; charges, refunds and disputes are updated in place; a few tables are hard-deleted under retention policies. Finance needs a daily figure that matches the source to the minor unit.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, shard counts and retention periods are hypothetical. Each shard has a primary and replicas; the change log exposes a monotonically increasing position per shard (an LSN or binlog position, depending on the engine).
sections.criteria: Consistent snapshot at a known log position with an idempotent overlap; per-key ordering by log position; deletes as tombstones that propagate; schema evolution under a contract with additive changes automatic and breaking changes blocked; a raw change table plus a merged current table; reconciliation with counts and sums per shard and day and a drill-down to keys; a plan for failover and log-retention gaps; protects the source.

clarifications.q: Do downstream users need every intermediate version of a row, or only the latest?
clarifications.a: Both: a current-state table for most users, and the full change history for audit.

clarifications.q: Is ordering needed across shards?
clarifications.a: No. Ordering per primary key within a shard is required; there is no global order across shards.

clarifications.q: Can we add columns or triggers to the source tables?
clarifications.a: No triggers. A product team may add columns, but you cannot ask them to change their write path.

clarifications.q: What happens on a shard failover?
clarifications.a: A replica is promoted. Your connector must survive it.

clarifications.q: Who consumes deletes?
clarifications.a: Retention deletes must propagate so the lakehouse does not keep data the source has removed.

hints: A snapshot and a stream overlap. Decide which log position the snapshot is consistent at, and what happens to changes made while it runs.
Order by the source's log position per shard, not by an updated_at column or by arrival time in the lakehouse.
Reconcile at a grain both sides can compute cheaply: counts and sums of amounts per table, shard and day, then drill down to keys.
followups: Walk through the snapshot-to-stream handoff for the {{largest_table}} table. Which rows can be seen twice, and why is that harmless in your design?
A row is updated twice within the same second. How does your merge pick the right version, and what breaks if you used updated_at instead?
A product team renames a column. What does each stage of your pipeline do, and who is alerted?
Finance's daily sum of net amounts differs from the source by 42 minor units for one shard. How do you find the cause?
The connector is down for longer than the {{log_retention}} log retention. What do you do, and how do you prove nothing was lost afterwards?

rules.ask: Two transactions commit in a different order from their updated_at values. Which version does your pipeline keep, and is it the committed one?
What is your partition key, and does it keep every change to one row in order through a shard failover?
Your MERGE sees a delete and an update for the same key in one batch. Which wins, and how do you know?
What does a full export cost at {{largest_table}}, and how fresh can it ever be?
Where does your exactly-once guarantee end, and what makes the lakehouse table correct beyond that point?

incidents: One of the {{shards}} shards fails over to a replica during peak, and for 4 minutes the connector reads a change log whose positions do not continue from the ones it checkpointed.
The connector falls behind and its oldest unread change is about to fall out of the {{log_retention}} log retention window.
A deploy adds a column to the refunds table with a default value, and the source rewrites every existing row.

templates.title: Idempotent payout pipeline
templates.subtopic: idempotency keys, state machines, bank files, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A payments platform pays merchants their available balance by bank transfer: about {{daily_payouts}} payouts a day through {{banks}} partner banks. Most banks take instructions as files with {{cutoffs}} submission cutoffs a day and send back acknowledgement and return files {{ack_delay}} later; some files arrive late, some twice, and some never. A payout sent twice is money lost to the platform; a payout never sent is a merchant who cannot make payroll.
sections.problem: Design the payout pipeline from "this merchant's balance is due" to "the bank confirmed or returned the money". Cover how a payout is created exactly once, its states and transitions, how instructions are built and submitted with retries, how acknowledgement and return files are ingested idempotently, the ledger entries at each step, reconciliation with the banks, and what you do with payouts whose outcome you do not know.
sections.constraints: A payout must never be sent twice and never silently dropped. Retries are certain: workers crash, submissions time out, files are re-sent. Merchant balances must stay consistent with the ledger at every step. Banks differ in file formats and in whether they accept a reference you provide.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, bank counts and delays are hypothetical. Public payments APIs document idempotency keys on create requests (a retried request with the same key returns the first result instead of creating a second object); you may use the same idea inside your own system.
sections.criteria: Payout created once under a deterministic idempotency key with a uniqueness constraint; explicit state machine with conditional transitions; attempts separate from payouts; an in-doubt state resolved by evidence, never by blind retry; idempotent file ingestion keyed by file and line identity; double-entry ledger entries that keep balances consistent through returns; daily reconciliation per bank with a human queue; honest about the bank boundary.

clarifications.q: Can a bank deduplicate on our reference?
clarifications.a: Some can, within a window; some cannot. Assume you cannot rely on it everywhere.

clarifications.q: Can a payout be cancelled after submission?
clarifications.a: Only until the bank's cutoff, and only with some banks.

clarifications.q: What is a return?
clarifications.a: The bank accepted the instruction but could not credit the account, for example a closed account, and sends the money back days later.

clarifications.q: How late can an acknowledgement be?
clarifications.a: Usually {{ack_delay}}; occasionally much later, and occasionally never.

clarifications.q: Who resolves a payout nobody can classify?
clarifications.a: An operations team, through a queue you design.

hints: Separate deciding to pay (one payout row, created under an idempotency key) from submitting (an attempt, which may happen more than once and must be recognisable).
Make every transition a conditional update from an expected state. A second worker that loses the race changes nothing.
"Submitted, and we do not know whether the bank has it" is a real state. Give it a name and a process.
followups: A worker submits a file and crashes before recording it. Walk through restart: how do you know whether that file reached the bank?
The same acknowledgement file arrives twice, and a different file acknowledges a payout you never sent. What does ingestion do with each?
A payout was confirmed, then returned five days later. What happens to the payout's state, the merchant's balance and the ledger?
Show the ledger entries for a payout that is created, submitted, confirmed and later returned, with amounts in minor units.
One bank's acknowledgements stop for a whole day across all {{cutoffs}} cutoffs. What do merchants see, what does operations do, and what must the system never do automatically?

rules.ask: Your retry fires after a timeout. How do you know the first attempt did not reach the bank, and what stops the retry from paying twice?
Inside your system you can be exactly once. What about the bank boundary, and what do you do when you cannot know?
The message is processed twice after a consumer rebalance. Which database write makes the second one harmless?
Two workers try to move the same payout from submitted to paid and to failed at the same time. What does the database see?
Nightly reconciliation finds a duplicate payout 20 hours after it was sent. What could you have caught earlier, and how?

incidents: A submission to one of the {{banks}} banks times out at the transport layer just before a cutoff; the file may or may not have arrived.
A bank re-sends the previous day's acknowledgement file with a new file name, and some lines now carry different statuses.
A deploy changes how the idempotency key is derived, and the scheduler re-creates payouts for 1 200 merchants that were already paid that morning.

templates.title: A double-entry ledger for money movement

sections.scenario: A payments platform moves money for merchants: a card charge credits the merchant and the platform's fee account, a refund and a payout debit the merchant, and a currency conversion moves value between currencies. Every movement must be explainable to an auditor for {{retention_years}} years. The platform posts about {{daily_journals}} journals a day across {{currencies}} currencies, and product teams want each merchant's available balance on demand.
sections.problem: Design the ledger's data model and its write path. Define accounts, journals and entries; how a journal is posted atomically and exactly once; how mistakes are corrected without editing history; how balances are served fast (snapshots taken {{snapshot_cadence}} plus the entries since); which invariants the system enforces, where, and how you prove they hold; and the queries an auditor will run.
sections.constraints: Posted entries are immutable: no UPDATE or DELETE on posted money. Every journal sums to zero in each currency. Amounts are integers in each currency's minor unit. A client may retry a posting after a timeout, and the retry must not move money twice. Balance reads p99 under 50 ms.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, latency targets and retention are hypothetical. Accounts belong to a merchant or to the platform (cash at banks, fees, FX clearing, reserves). Payment-processor terms such as "balance transaction" are used in their public meaning: one record of a movement through an account balance, with amount, fee and net in minor units.
sections.criteria: Journal/entry separation with signed integer minor units; per-currency zero-sum enforced synchronously on write and re-verified asynchronously; immutability with reversals and links; idempotent posting with a stored request fingerprint; snapshot + tail with a precise watermark; hot-account mitigation; effective time distinct from recorded time; audit queries named; each incident handled with containment, correction by compensating journals, and a guardrail.

clarifications.q: Is a negative balance allowed?
clarifications.a: For some account types yes (a merchant can go negative after a refund); for platform cash accounts it is an alert, not a constraint violation.

clarifications.q: Do journals ever touch more than two accounts?
clarifications.a: Yes. A charge has at least three legs (cash, merchant, fees); a conversion has four, two per currency.

clarifications.q: What does a client send to make a posting safe to retry?
clarifications.a: An idempotency key per logical operation, the same pattern public payment APIs document for POST requests.

clarifications.q: Can a journal be backdated?
clarifications.a: Only with an explicit effective time; the time it was recorded is always kept as well.

clarifications.q: Who reads the ledger?
clarifications.a: The balance API, finance close, reconciliation against bank statements, and auditors.

hints: Separate the journal (one business event, atomic) from its entries (one signed amount per account per currency). The invariant lives on the journal.
A correction is a new journal: a reversal that negates the original, then the right posting. Link them.
A balance is a cached fold over entries. Decide what the snapshot covers (up to which entry or which time) so that snapshot + tail is always exact.
followups: Where exactly is the "sums to zero per currency" invariant enforced: in the database, in the posting service, or by an asynchronous checker? What does each catch that the others miss?
One platform account (fees in the main currency) is touched by most journals. What happens to write contention, and how do you remove the hot row without breaking the balance?
An auditor asks for one merchant's balance as of the end of last quarter, as it was reported then, and as it is known now after backdated corrections. What do you store to answer both?
The ledger must be split across shards by account. A journal now spans shards. How do you keep posting atomic and the invariant true?
Prove to finance, every day, that no entry was lost or duplicated between the ledger and the warehouse copy.

rules.ask: Two postings to the same account commit at the same moment. Show how your balance stays correct, and what the row lock does to throughput on the fees account.
The constraint says posted money is immutable. How would you correct a wrong amount without UPDATE, and what does the auditor see afterwards?
Why integers in minor units? What breaks with floating point, and how do you handle a currency whose minor unit is not 1/100?
The retry arrives with the same key but a different amount. What does your posting API return, and how long do you keep keys?
Is the event log your ledger, or does it feed one? Where is the invariant checked before money is considered posted?

incidents: The nightly invariant check finds 1,800 journals in one zero-decimal currency that do not sum to zero; all came through a bulk import path that bypassed the posting service. They have already been folded into the balance snapshots taken {{snapshot_cadence}}.
A client timed out on a payout posting and retried with a new idempotency key: the merchant's payout was journaled twice and the second one has already been sent to the bank.
After a backfill of backdated entries, the balance API (snapshot plus tail) and a full recomputation from entries disagree for 40 merchant accounts.

templates.title: The payment intent lifecycle, from OLTP to facts
templates.subtopic: state machines, event models, accumulating snapshots

sections.scenario: A merchant integration creates a payment intent for each checkout. The intent moves through a lifecycle: it requires a payment method, may require customer action (for example an authentication step, about {{action_share}} of intents here), moves to processing, and ends succeeded or canceled; a failed attempt sends it back to requiring a payment method. About {{daily_intents}} intents are created a day. Merchants receive state changes as webhook events, which can arrive late (up to {{webhook_lag}} here), more than once, and out of order, as public payment API documentation warns.
sections.problem: Model the lifecycle three ways and say how they connect: (1) the OLTP state machine, with its allowed transitions and how a transition is recorded; (2) the event model (what one event carries and how a consumer applies it safely); (3) the analytical facts that answer "conversion from created to succeeded by day, merchant and payment method", "time spent in requires_action" and "how many intents are stuck in processing right now". Choose between an accumulating snapshot fact and a transaction (event) fact, or justify both.
sections.constraints: The analytical model must be correct when events arrive out of order or twice. A terminal state is never left. Conversion is reported by the day the intent was created, and that number must stop changing after a defined close.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and lags are hypothetical. Public documentation lists further statuses (for example requires_confirmation and requires_capture); they are in scope if you include them. Every event carries the object's id, the new status, an event id and the time the event was created.
sections.criteria: Explicit state machine with legal transitions and terminal states; idempotent, order-tolerant consumer (event-id dedup, transition legality or rank-based rebuild); a transaction fact for intervals and attempts plus an accumulating snapshot (or current-state table) for outcome and stuck queries, with the trade-off stated; creation-day attribution with a close and a provisional label; schema evolution of states; each incident diagnosed with the right model.

clarifications.q: Which states are terminal?
clarifications.a: succeeded and canceled. A failed payment attempt is not terminal: the intent returns to requires_payment_method.

clarifications.q: Can an intent pass through requires_action more than once?
clarifications.a: Yes, after a failed attempt and a new payment method.

clarifications.q: Do I get a sequence number per intent?
clarifications.a: No. You get the event's created time (second precision) and the event id; two events can share a second.

clarifications.q: Do analysts need every attempt or only the outcome?
clarifications.a: Both: conversion needs the outcome, and decline analysis needs each attempt.

clarifications.q: How long can an intent stay open?
clarifications.a: Days. An abandoned intent may never reach a terminal state unless the merchant cancels it.

hints: An accumulating snapshot has one row per intent with a column per milestone, updated as milestones arrive. A transaction fact has one row per transition and is append-only.
Out-of-order events: apply a transition only if it is legal from the current state, or rebuild the current state from the full event set ordered by a rank you define.
"Stuck in processing" is a question about the current state; "time in requires_action" is a question about intervals. Different grains.
followups: A succeeded event arrives before the processing event for the same intent. Walk through your consumer and both facts.
Define the close: when is a creation day's conversion final, given intents can stay open for days? What do you show before that?
The same event is delivered three times during a backlog of {{webhook_lag}}. Prove your facts count it once.
Product adds a new status between processing and succeeded. What breaks in each of your three models, and how do you roll it out without rewriting history?
At {{daily_intents}} a day, the accumulating snapshot is updated in place. How do you store it so updates stay cheap in a columnar warehouse?

rules.ask: Your snapshot row is updated each time a milestone lands. How do you keep a late duplicate event from overwriting a later milestone with an earlier one?
How does an analyst get "intents currently in processing" from an append-only fact without scanning all history?
Two events for one intent share the same second. Which one wins, and why is "latest timestamp wins" unsafe for a terminal state?
A stale requires_action event arrives after succeeded. What does your merge do, and what stops it?

incidents: The webhook consumer was down for {{webhook_lag}}; on recovery it receives the backlog with retries interleaved, and the "stuck in processing" dashboard pages the on-call team for 40,000 intents that actually succeeded.
A merchant integration bug confirms some intents twice; the warehouse now shows {{action_share}} more requires_action entries than authentication attempts recorded upstream.
Yesterday's conversion rate, already sent to a merchant, changes by 0.7 points overnight as late terminal events land.

templates.title: Dispute lifecycle and win-rate reporting
templates.subtopic: lifecycle history, SCD versus event sourcing, deadlines

fee_rule: is charged when a chargeback opens (never for an inquiry) and returned if the dispute is won
is charged when a chargeback opens (never for an inquiry) and kept whatever the outcome

sections.scenario: A cardholder can question a payment with their issuer. Sometimes this starts as an inquiry (a request for information that is not yet a chargeback); often it starts as a chargeback directly. The merchant may submit evidence before a deadline, here {{evidence_days}} days, after which the issuer decides: won or lost. In this scenario a dispute fee {{fee_rule}}. Disputes arrive from {{networks}} card networks, about {{monthly_disputes}} a month, and merchants want win rates they can act on.
sections.problem: Design the data model for disputes: the lifecycle (inquiry → chargeback → evidence submitted → under review → won or lost, including an inquiry that closes without escalating), deadlines, the money movements (the disputed amount withdrawn, the fee, and any amount returned on a win), the links to the original charge and to refunds on that charge, and the history needed to answer "what state was this dispute in on any date". Then define the win-rate metric precisely and the model that serves it by month, network, reason and merchant.
sections.constraints: Win rate must be reproducible: last month's published number may change only by a documented restatement. Every money movement reconciles to the ledger. Missing an evidence deadline must be detectable before it happens.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, deadlines and the fee rule are hypothetical; real deadlines and fees vary by network and region. A charge can have several partial refunds and at most one open dispute at a time. Network reason codes are mapped to a small internal set of reasons.
sections.criteria: Clean separation of entity, history and money; explicit inquiry and chargeback stages; deadlines stored with their source time zone; links to charge and refunds that make total cost per charge answerable; history that supports state-as-of-date and late corrections; a precise, cohort-based win-rate definition with a restatement policy; reason-code mapping as versioned data; each incident resolved with the history and ledger intact.

clarifications.q: Does an inquiry count in the win rate?
clarifications.a: Not as a chargeback. Report inquiries separately, with their own escalation rate.

clarifications.q: What if the merchant refunds after the dispute opens?
clarifications.a: In this scenario the refund does not close the dispute; both can move money, so double loss is possible and must be visible.

clarifications.q: Does a dispute's amount always equal the charge amount?
clarifications.a: No. A dispute can be partial, and the charge may already be partly refunded.

clarifications.q: Win rate by which month: opened or closed?
clarifications.a: You decide, but say why and keep it consistent.

clarifications.q: Can a decision be reversed?
clarifications.a: Rarely, through a later network stage. Model it so that it is possible.

hints: Separate the dispute entity (current state, keys, deadline) from its history (one row per transition with an effective time), and from the money (ledger journals that reference the dispute).
A win rate needs a cohort and a denominator. "Won / (won + lost)" over disputes opened in a month, counted once closed, is one defensible definition; say what you do with still-open disputes.
A type-2 dimension and an event-sourced history can answer the same "state on date X" question. Compare what each costs to correct.
followups: Write the definition of win rate you would publish, including what happens to disputes still open at month end and to inquiries that escalate.
A network sends the "won" decision, then a correction 3 days later saying "lost". What happens in your history, your ledger and your published win rate?
Show how a merchant support agent answers "how much did this one charge cost us in total": charge, refunds, dispute amount, fee and any return.
The deadline alert must fire 48 hours before {{evidence_days}}-day deadlines across time zones. Where does the deadline live and in which time zone?
At {{monthly_disputes}} disputes a month and {{networks}} networks with their own codes, how do you keep the reason mapping stable when a network adds codes?

rules.ask: A decision arrives with an effective time earlier than the last version's valid_from. How does your type-2 table absorb it without overlapping intervals?
An analyst wants the state of 1 million disputes on 30 June. Does your design replay events for each query, or keep a projection?
Your denominator includes disputes still under review. What does that do to the newest month, and how will a merchant misread it?
How do you answer "how long did this dispute spend under review" if the status column is overwritten?

incidents: The {{evidence_days}}-day deadline was computed in UTC for one network whose deadline is defined in another time zone; 300 disputes were auto-marked expired a day early.
A network sends a batch of corrections reversing 2% of last month's "won" decisions after the monthly win-rate report went to merchants.
Finance finds disputes where a fee was debited twice, once at the inquiry and again when it escalated to a chargeback, although the fee rule says it {{fee_rule}}.

templates.title: Multi-currency balances and FX for reporting
templates.subtopic: minor units, effective-dated FX rates, restatement

report: monthly gross volume by merchant country
quarterly net revenue by product line

sections.scenario: Customers pay in their own currency (the presentment currency) and merchants can be settled in a different one (the settlement currency); the conversion happens at a rate on the day of the charge. The platform supports {{currencies}} currencies, including zero-decimal currencies (such as JPY) and three-decimal currencies (such as KWD). Leadership wants {{report}} in {{reporting_currency}}, and finance wants to know how much of a month-over-month change is real volume and how much is currency movement.
sections.problem: Design the data model for amounts, currencies and FX rates, and the reporting layer on top. Cover: how an amount is stored (minor units and per-currency exponents), the FX rate table as effective-dated data published {{rate_cadence}}, the difference between the rate applied to a transaction (a fact about that transaction) and the rate used for reporting (a policy), rounding rules and where they apply, and how a report is restated when a rate or an exponent was wrong.
sections.constraints: No floating point anywhere money is stored. A transaction's settlement amount never changes after it is recorded. Reports are reproducible: re-running last quarter's report gives last quarter's number unless a restatement is published. Totals in {{reporting_currency}} must reconcile, within a stated rounding tolerance, with the sum of converted lines.
sections.assumptions: Currency counts, cadence and report choices are hypothetical. A currency's exponent can change (a redenomination) but rarely; the rate source can publish a correction.
sections.criteria: Integer minor units with an effective-dated exponent table; FX rates as bitemporal data (valid-from and published-at); applied rate stored on the transaction, reporting rate as a named policy; explicit rounding step and tolerance; constant-currency decomposition; reproducible reports with explicit restatement; each incident traced to the affected rows, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Which rate converts a transaction for the report?
clarifications.a: Your choice: the rate actually applied, the rate on the transaction date, or a month-average rate. Say which report uses which and why.

clarifications.q: Do rates come with a valid-from time?
clarifications.a: Yes, and corrections arrive as new rows for the same valid-from time with a later published time.

clarifications.q: Round per line or per total?
clarifications.a: Decide, and state the tolerance between the two.

clarifications.q: Is the conversion fee part of the rate?
clarifications.a: Model it separately; reporting wants a rate without fees.

clarifications.q: What precision do rates have?
clarifications.a: Up to 10 significant digits; store them exactly.

hints: Store amount_minor BIGINT plus currency, and keep the exponent in a currency table with its own valid-from date. Never store a decimal amount as the source of truth.
A rate table keyed by (base, quote, valid_from, published_at) answers both "the rate we believed then" and "the corrected rate now".
Constant-currency reporting (this period's volume at last period's rates) separates volume change from FX change.
followups: Write the join that picks "the rate in force at the transaction time, as published by the report's cut-off". What index makes it cheap?
A three-decimal currency was loaded with exponent 2 for six weeks. How do you find every affected number, and what do you restate?
Show how to split month-over-month change in {{reporting_currency}} into volume and FX effects.
Line-level rounding and total-level rounding disagree by 3 units of {{reporting_currency}} on a report. Which is right, and what do you print?
The rate source publishes a correction to one of last Tuesday's {{rate_cadence}} rates. Which reports change, which must not, and how does a reader tell?

rules.ask: What does 0.1 + 0.2 do to a ledger total, and how would your design guarantee integers end to end?
A report for last quarter is re-run today. With "latest rate", does it give the same answer as when it was published?
Where does the average come from, and how do you reconcile a month-average report with the settlement amounts finance books?
At which step do you round, and what tolerance do you publish between the sum of rounded lines and the rounded total?

incidents: One {{rate_cadence}} publication carried a wrong rate for one currency (off by a factor of 100); transactions converted at it are already in the draft of {{report}} that went to leadership.
A three-decimal currency's exponent was loaded as 2, so its volumes in {{reporting_currency}} were 10 times too high for six weeks.
Finance's {{reporting_currency}} total and the sum of the per-merchant lines in the report differ by more than the published rounding tolerance after a currency was added mid-month.

templates.title: Ledger queries — quarantine unbalanced journals, balances as of a time
templates.subtopic: double-entry invariants, as-of balances, bitemporal filters

sections.scenario: A double-entry ledger stores each money movement as a journal (one business event) with several entries (one signed amount per account and currency). A positive amount_minor is a debit, a negative one a credit, and every journal should sum to zero in each currency. A buggy import has let some unbalanced journals in. Finance wants each account's balance at a point in time, with unbalanced journals held aside rather than silently posted.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns account_id, currency, balance_minor, unbalanced_journals: one row per (account_id, currency) that has at least one entry in an eligible journal, ordered by account_id, currency. {{time_rule}} A journal is unbalanced in a currency when its entries in that currency do not sum to zero. balance_minor is the sum of amount_minor over the account's entries in that currency from eligible journals, leaving out entries of journals that are unbalanced in that currency. unbalanced_journals is the number of distinct eligible journals, unbalanced in that currency, that have an entry for the account in that currency. {{currency_rule}} {{reversal_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Time boundaries are inclusive. A row whose balance is 0 is still returned. The sample has {{journals}} journals and {{entries}} entries; production has billions of entries.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, accounts and amounts. cash, fees and fx_clearing are platform accounts; merchant_* accounts belong to merchants. Balances are reported in each currency's minor unit, never converted.
sections.criteria: Eligibility decided per journal with inclusive boundaries (and, at the hardest level, effective time with a known-at cut-off); balance check grouped by journal and currency; unbalanced entries excluded from the balance but counted; reversals treated as ordinary journals; zero rows kept; deterministic ordering; can explain snapshots and write-time enforcement.

clarifications.q: Is balance "debits minus credits"?
clarifications.a: Yes: the signed sum of amount_minor, with debits positive.

clarifications.q: If a journal is unbalanced in one currency but balanced in another, what happens to its entries in the balanced currency?
clarifications.a: They count. Balance is checked per journal per currency.

clarifications.q: Should an account whose entries all cancel, or are all held aside, appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with balance_minor 0.

clarifications.q: Is a journal at exactly the as-of time included?
clarifications.a: Yes. Boundaries are inclusive.

clarifications.q: Does the reversal of a journal make the original disappear?
clarifications.a: No. Both are journals; each counts when it is itself eligible.

hints: Decide eligibility once, at the journal level, in its own CTE. Every entry of a journal shares its timestamps.
Check balance with GROUP BY journal_id, currency over eligible entries, then join that verdict back to the entries.
SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE ...) and COUNT(DISTINCT ...) FILTER (WHERE ...) produce both output columns in one pass.
followups: At billions of entries, this query recomputes every balance from the beginning. How would balance snapshots change it, and what makes snapshot + tail exact when backdated journals arrive?
Turn the unbalanced-journal check into a write-time guarantee. Where does it run, and what does the posting API return when it fails?
Finance wants the balance "as of effective time T, as known at K" for every month end of last year. How do you store and index the ledger so that is cheap?
An auditor asks you to prove the quarantined journals were never visible in a merchant's available balance. What evidence do you produce?

rules.ask: Did you group by currency too? What does a currency conversion journal look like to your check?
Which timestamp decides whether a backdated journal is in the balance, and when does created_at still matter?
You are excluding reversed journals. What is the balance one minute before the reversal was posted?
Your HAVING clause filters rows. Which accounts disappear from the report, and should they?

incidents: The quarantined journals in this report come from a bulk import that bypassed the posting service. Finance asks whether merchants could have withdrawn against them, and the balance API has no notion of quarantine.

After a correction batch posts reversals with effective times earlier than their creation, last month's closing balances recomputed today no longer match the balances finance reported, and finance asks which number is right.

templates.title: Real-time payments analytics for merchants

sections.scenario: A payments platform processes about {{daily_payments}} payments a day for {{merchants}} merchants, in {{currencies}} presentment currencies. Each payment moves through states (created, authorized, succeeded or failed, later perhaps refunded or disputed), and every movement of money creates a balance transaction with an amount, a fee and a net, all integers in the currency's minor unit. Merchants want a dashboard that shows gross volume, net volume, payment success rate, refunds, disputes and upcoming payouts, fresh within {{freshness}}. Their finance teams compare the same numbers with payout reports, so totals must agree to the minor unit.
sections.problem: Design the analytics platform behind this dashboard. Cover the events or change stream you consume, how you aggregate exactly, how you compute success rate, how you handle currencies and merchant time zones, where the numbers are stored and served, how merchants (and platforms that manage connected accounts) are isolated from one another, and how the dashboard is reconciled with the ledger.
sections.constraints: Money totals are exact integers in minor units; floating point is not allowed anywhere on the money path. A merchant sees only its own data; a platform sees its connected accounts and nothing else. Dashboard queries p95 under 1 second, including for the largest merchants. Intraday numbers may lag by up to {{freshness}} but must never double count; once a day is final it must equal the ledger exactly.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and SLOs are hypothetical. The ledger (balance transactions) is the financial source of truth and can be read as an ordered change stream. Payment-state events are a separate stream and may arrive out of order.
sections.criteria: Uses the ledger as the source of truth for money and keeps state events for rates; exact integer arithmetic in minor units; idempotent aggregation keyed by the ledger identifier; numerators and denominators stored, never rates; time-zone-safe buckets; explicit as-of labelling and a finalisation step reconciled with the ledger; tenant isolation including platforms; hot-merchant handling; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is success rate measured per attempt or per payment?
clarifications.a: Both are useful; the dashboard's headline is per payment (did the customer eventually pay), with attempt-level detail for debugging declines. You must define both.

clarifications.q: Which currency are totals shown in?
clarifications.a: In each settlement currency, plus a converted total in the merchant's default currency that is labelled as converted.

clarifications.q: Which day does a payment belong to?
clarifications.a: The merchant's reporting time zone, which the merchant can change.

clarifications.q: Do refunds and disputes reduce gross volume?
clarifications.a: No. Gross volume counts successful payments; net volume subtracts refunds, dispute amounts and fees.

clarifications.q: How late can a change arrive?
clarifications.a: Most within seconds. A dispute or refund can arrive months after the payment, and it belongs to the day it happened, not the payment's day.

hints: Sums and counts are mergeable and can be exact; rates are not. Store numerator and denominator, and divide at read time.
Make every aggregation idempotent on the ledger's own identifier so a replayed change cannot count twice.
Hourly UTC buckets cannot be rolled up into a day in every time zone. Some offsets are not whole hours.
followups: How do you compute success rate so that a customer who fails twice and then succeeds counts as one successful payment, and why can you not average per-hour success rates?
A merchant changes its reporting time zone. What has to be recomputed, and what does the merchant see while that happens?
A platform with 400,000 connected accounts opens its dashboard. How do you serve a total across all of them in under a second?
The finalised total for one merchant-day differs from the ledger by 312 minor units. Walk through how you find the cause.
Converted totals use FX rates. Which rate do you use, when is it fixed, and what changes if the rate for a past day is corrected?

rules.ask: Where in your design does a money value stop being an integer of minor units, and what error does that introduce at a billion rows?
One merchant runs a flash sale and sends 15% of all payments. What happens to the partition and to every other merchant on it?
Why is the average of hourly success rates not the daily success rate?
Exactly-once inside the stream processor does not cover the sink. What makes the write to your serving store idempotent?
A merchant reports in UTC+05:30. How does your hourly bucket give them a correct day?

incidents: A single merchant runs a flash sale and sends 15% of all payments for two hours. The stream partition holding that merchant falls 20 minutes behind, so every merchant on it sees a dashboard older than the {{freshness}} promise.
A change-data-capture connector restarts from an old offset and re-emits the last 3 hours of balance transactions. Volume for the affected merchants doubles on the dashboard.
A merchant whose reporting time zone is UTC+05:30 says yesterday's gross volume on the dashboard does not match the payout report they downloaded.
The FX rate feed stalls for 90 minutes; converted totals across {{currencies}} currencies are still being computed with the last rate received.

templates.title: Webhook delivery at scale

sections.scenario: A payments API notifies merchants of events (a payment succeeded, a refund was created, a dispute was opened, a payout was paid) by sending an HTTPS POST to endpoints the merchants register. There are {{endpoints}} registered endpoints, each subscribed to some event types, and the platform produces about {{events_per_sec}} events per second at peak. A platform account can receive events for all of its connected accounts at one endpoint. At any moment about {{down_share}} of endpoints are failing; some are slow, some return errors, and some are down for days.
sections.problem: Design the delivery system. Cover how an event becomes one delivery per subscribed endpoint, how deliveries are scheduled and retried with backoff for up to {{retry_days}} days, what delivery guarantee you give and what you tell merchants about ordering, how one slow or dead endpoint is kept from hurting everyone else, how you apply backpressure, and what a merchant can see and do (delivery logs, manual resend).
sections.constraints: Delivery is at least once. Healthy endpoints should receive events within a few seconds at p99, whatever other endpoints are doing. Endpoint URLs are supplied by merchants and are untrusted. Each payload is signed so the receiver can verify it and reject replays. After {{retry_days}} days of failure, an event is no longer retried automatically.
sections.assumptions: All rates and counts are hypothetical. Events are already durably written to an internal event log before delivery starts. Receivers are expected to respond quickly with a 2xx and do their work asynchronously.
sections.criteria: Durable event log → per-endpoint delivery records with stable identity; at-least-once with event ids for receiver dedup, and an honest ordering story (object state can be fetched, events carry created times); retries with capped exponential backoff and jitter, slowing for long-dead endpoints, within {{retry_days}} days; per-endpoint concurrency, timeouts and circuit breakers; fair scheduling and isolation of slow endpoints; controlled ramp-up on recovery; SSRF protection and signed payloads with timestamps; delivery logs and replay; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do you guarantee ordering?
clarifications.a: Not across events. Decide what you can offer, and what you tell merchants to do instead.

clarifications.q: What counts as success?
clarifications.a: Any 2xx within the timeout. Anything else, including a timeout or a redirect, is a failure.

clarifications.q: Can a merchant replay old events?
clarifications.a: Yes, for events in the last {{retry_days}} days, from the dashboard or the API.

clarifications.q: What happens to an endpoint that fails for the whole retry window?
clarifications.a: Product wants the merchant notified, and the endpoint eventually disabled. You decide the policy.

clarifications.q: Can one event go to several endpoints?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each subscribed endpoint gets its own delivery with its own retry state.

hints: Separate the fan-out (event → deliveries) from the delivery workers, and give every delivery an identity that survives retries.
One physical queue per endpoint does not scale to millions; one shared queue lets a dead endpoint block everyone. Find the middle.
Workers waiting on hung connections are the scarce resource. Timeouts and concurrency limits are per endpoint, not global.
followups: A merchant receives the same event twice and charges their customer's order twice in their own system. What did you promise, and what do you give them to prevent it?
An endpoint receives "refund created" before "payment succeeded" for the same payment. Is that a bug? What would you do if a large merchant insists on order?
An endpoint has been failing for two days. How often do you retry now, where do its pending deliveries live, and what does it cost you?
How do you stop a merchant from registering an endpoint that points at an address inside your own network?
The delivery fleet itself must be deployed without losing or doubling deliveries in flight. How?

rules.ask: The receiver can time out after processing your POST. How can a delivery over HTTP be exactly once, and what do you promise instead?
Strict ordering means one failing event blocks every later event for that merchant. Is that what the merchant wants?
With {{endpoints}} endpoints, what does a physical queue per endpoint cost in brokers, file handles and rebalancing?
After a regional network blip, a million endpoints recover at the same moment. What does your retry schedule do to them?
Fifteen percent of endpoints start hanging until the timeout. What fraction of your workers are waiting, and what happens to healthy endpoints?

incidents: A hosting provider used by about 15% of endpoints starts accepting connections and then hanging until the timeout. Delivery workers spend their time waiting, and delivery latency for healthy endpoints rises from seconds to 40 minutes.
A large platform's endpoint, which receives events for all of its connected accounts, has been down for two of the {{retry_days}} retry days and holds a backlog equal to two days of its traffic.
When that endpoint comes back, the whole backlog is released at once and the platform's servers fall over again within a minute.
A merchant says a payment-succeeded event never arrived and their logs show nothing. Your delivery record says it was delivered with a 200.

templates.title: Settlement reconciliation platform
templates.subtopic: reconciliation, late and corrected data, auditability

sections.scenario: A payments company records every movement of money in its own double-entry ledger.
