Each day {{sources}} external parties (card processors, acquirers and banks) send settlement files that say what they actually settled: gross amounts, fees, chargebacks, adjustments and the net transfer. Together the files hold about {{daily_lines}} lines a day. Most arrive the next morning; some arrive {{late_days}} days late; some are later reissued with corrections. Finance must close each month within {{close_days}} business days, and every unmatched difference needs an owner and an age.
sections.problem: Design the reconciliation platform. Cover file ingestion and versioning, normalising very different formats, generating expectations from the ledger, the matching rules (one to one, one to many, many to one, tolerances), the states a record can be in, the exceptions queue with ownership and aging, how late and corrected files are handled without rewriting history, and what finance sees at month-end.
sections.constraints: Amounts are exact, in minor units, and currencies have different exponents (some have none, some have three). Nothing that was reported in a closed month may change silently; a correction after close is a visible adjustment. Every match must be explainable: which rule, which records, which file version. The platform must show what it knew on any past date.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and timings are hypothetical. The internal ledger is immutable: corrections are new entries, never edits. External files are trusted only after validation (checksums, row counts, totals in the trailer where present).
sections.criteria: Immutable raw landing with file identity (hash, source, date, version) and validation; normalised record model with exact minor-unit amounts and currency exponents; expectations from the ledger so missing files surface; ordered, explainable matching rules including one-to-many and many-to-one with tolerances that are explicit and approved; supersede-and-rematch for corrections with bitemporal history; aging from expected date with per-source grace; exceptions workflow with owners and reason codes; month-end view and post-close adjustments; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do external lines carry our identifiers?
clarifications.a: Some do (a reference we sent with the transaction); some only carry amount, date, card fragment and the network's own reference. Expect both.

clarifications.q: Does every source settle per transaction?
clarifications.a: No. Some send one net line per batch, with fees deducted, which must match many ledger entries.

clarifications.q: When is a record an exception?
clarifications.a: When it is not matched by its expected settlement date plus a grace period that differs by source.

clarifications.q: Who works the exceptions?
clarifications.a: A finance operations team of a few dozen people, who need assignments, reason codes and a history.

clarifications.q: Is a missing file an exception?
clarifications.a: Yes. The platform must notice a file that never arrived, not just lines that do not match.

hints: Reconcile against expectations: derive from the ledger what each source should send and when, so silence is detectable.
Treat each file version as immutable and make matches point at record versions. A correction then becomes "supersede and re-match", not "update".
Order the rules from strict to loose, and record which rule made each match.
followups: A processor settles one net line per day per currency, after fees and chargebacks. How do you match it to tens of thousands of ledger entries, and what do you do when it is off by a small amount?
A corrected file arrives for a settlement date in a month that is already closed. What changes, what does not, and what does finance see?
How do you define aging so that a file arriving {{late_days}} days late does not flood the queue with false exceptions, but a truly missing settlement still surfaces?
An auditor asks: "Show me the reconciliation state as of the close of March, and every change since." How does your model answer?
Matching is now 6 hours for a day's files and close is at risk. Where does the time go and how do you parallelise it safely?

rules.ask: Finance closed last month on the old values. After your update, how do you show what they closed on?
Two ledger entries have the same amount and date. How do you avoid matching the wrong one, and how would anyone know?
A full outer join tells you what did not match today. How do you tell a record that will match tomorrow from one that never will?
One source rounds fees per batch and another per transaction. How does your matching treat a one-minor-unit difference, and who signs off on it?
The file for the last day of the month arrives after close has started. Does your nightly job see it, and what decides whether that day is re-matched?

incidents: One of the {{sources}} sources delivers the same settlement file twice under different file names. Unmatched external lines jump by exactly that file's line count.

A bank's settlement file for the last day of the month arrives {{late_days}} days late. Until it does, the exceptions queue fills with ledger entries that look unmatched, and finance must decide whether to close within {{close_days}} business days without it.
A processor reissues a corrected file for a settlement date that was in last month's close; 3% of its lines change amount.
A processor starts reporting fees once per batch instead of per transaction, and thousands of matches now differ by one minor unit.

templates.title: Fraud feature platform for authorization
templates.subtopic: online-offline consistency, point-in-time correctness, low latency

entities: card, email address and IP address

sections.scenario: A payments platform scores every payment attempt for fraud before it is sent for authorization, at up to {{auth_tps}} attempts per second. The model uses velocity features: for each of {{entities}}, counts and amounts of attempts, declines and distinct counterparts (for example distinct cards seen on one IP address) over windows of {{windows}}. The fraud team trains new models every week on historical attempts. Fraud labels arrive late: a cardholder dispute can come weeks after the payment.
sections.problem: Design the feature platform. The online path must return the feature vector within {{budget_ms}} ms at p99 inside the authorization path. The offline path must produce training rows whose features equal what the model would have seen at decision time. Cover feature definitions, the streaming computation, the online store, how the current attempt is treated, point-in-time correct training data, label handling, monitoring of online-offline skew, and what happens when part of the system is slow or down.
sections.constraints: A feature fetch slower than {{budget_ms}} ms at p99 is a failure; the payment must still be decided. A feature must have one definition used by both paths. Training data must never contain information from after the decision. Raw card numbers never enter the feature platform; cards are identified by a fingerprint or token.
sections.assumptions: All rates, budgets and windows are hypothetical. Attempts arrive on an event log with an event time and an attempt id. Declined and blocked attempts are logged as well as successful ones.
sections.criteria: One declarative feature definition compiled for stream and batch; bucketed window counters in a low-latency store with bounded reads; an explicit rule for the current attempt and in-flight events, shared by both paths; logging of served features and training on them; point-in-time as-of joins for backfills; label maturity handling; hot-key protection and graceful degradation with missingness the model was trained on; skew monitoring; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a velocity count include the attempt being scored?
clarifications.a: You decide, but online and offline must make the same choice.

clarifications.q: Do declined attempts count?
clarifications.a: Yes. Repeated declines are among the strongest signals, for example in card testing.

clarifications.q: Can distinct counts be approximate?
clarifications.a: Yes, within a stated error, if training uses the same approximation.

clarifications.q: How late are labels?
clarifications.a: Most disputes arrive within a few weeks; some take months. Training must account for that.

clarifications.q: What if the feature store is unavailable?
clarifications.a: The payment is still scored, with whatever features are present, and the response says which were missing.

hints: The simplest way to make training match serving is to log the exact feature vector that was served, keyed by attempt id, and train on that.
For new features there is no log yet, so you still need a point-in-time backfill: an as-of join on event time that uses only events strictly before the decision.
Sliding windows over long periods are expensive per event. Bucketed counters (per minute for an hour, per hour for days) bound the cost.
followups: Precisely which events are counted in "attempts on this card in the last hour" at decision time, online and offline? Include the attempt itself, concurrent attempts, and events still in flight in the stream.
A new feature needs two years of history before it can be trained. How do you backfill it so it equals what the online path will compute from now on?
During a card-testing attack one IP address has 40,000 attempts in ten minutes. What happens to its counters, its distinct-card set and your read latency?
How do you build labels for a weekly training run when disputes for the last month are still arriving?
How do you detect, in production, that an online feature has drifted from its offline definition, and what do you page on?

rules.ask: Your offline job sees events that were still in the stream when the online decision was made. How do you make offline see only what online saw?
The hot key for one IP address now takes 80% of one shard's traffic. What do you do within the {{budget_ms}} ms budget?
Training used exact distinct counts but serving uses a sketch. What does that mismatch do to the model?
Counting a week of attempts at request time inside {{budget_ms}} ms at {{auth_tps}} per second: show the arithmetic.
When features are missing, what does the model receive, and was it trained to see that?

incidents: A card-testing attack sends 40,000 small attempts in ten minutes from a handful of IP addresses, each with a different card. The shard holding those keys pushes p99 feature latency past {{budget_ms}} ms for every payment on it.
A deploy of the streaming job stalls it for 15 minutes, longer than the shortest of its windows ({{windows}}). Velocity features read stale counts while it catches up.
A backfill of last quarter's training set disagrees with the logged decision-time values on 6% of rows.
The online store in one region fails over to a replica that is 20 seconds behind, and every counter on it loses its last 20 seconds of updates.

templates.title: Multi-region available-balance service

sections.scenario: A payments platform keeps a balance for each of {{accounts}} merchant accounts. Incoming payments add pending funds that become available after settlement; payouts, refunds and transfers debit the available balance. Debit requests arrive at up to {{debits_per_sec}} per second across {{regions}} regions. A double-entry ledger is the source of truth for money; the balance is what the system checks before it lets a debit through. An account must not be overdrawn by a debit the platform approved, and the platform must keep working when one region is lost for {{outage}}.
sections.problem: Design the balance service. Cover the relation between the ledger and the balance, how a debit is checked and applied atomically, where each account's authoritative state lives, how writes are replicated, what happens to debits and credits for an account when a region is unreachable, how idempotency survives failover, and how you prove the balances are right. Be explicit about which guarantees you give up, when, and why.
sections.constraints: No approved debit may take available balance below zero (a small, explicitly bounded exception is allowed only if you justify it and the business accepts it). Every balance change corresponds to balanced ledger entries. Debit requests carry an idempotency key; a retried request must never apply twice, even if the retry lands in a different region. Debit p99 latency under 300 ms.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, latencies and outage durations are hypothetical. Inter-region round trips are tens of milliseconds. Credits from settlement arrive in batches; debits arrive one at a time from the API.
sections.criteria: Ledger as the source of truth with balanced entries; the balance as a derived, transactionally maintained projection; one serialisation point per account (home region with synchronous replication or consensus) or explicit escrow splits; idempotency records committed atomically with the debit and replicated with it; a clear CAP position per operation (credits accepted and applied later, debits refused or capped by pre-allocated allowances during a partition); correct quorum reasoning for {{regions}} regions; hot-account sharding; continuous invariant checks; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the balance be eventually consistent?
clarifications.a: For display, yes. For the overdraft check, you must explain exactly what consistency the check reads.

clarifications.q: Must a debit succeed during a regional outage?
clarifications.a: The business wants as many as possible to succeed, but not at the cost of unbounded overdrafts. Propose the trade.

clarifications.q: Are holds supported?
clarifications.a: Yes. Some flows reserve funds first and then capture or release them.

clarifications.q: Is the ledger in one region?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design. It must not lose a committed entry if a region is lost.

clarifications.q: How hot can one account be?
clarifications.a: Most are quiet; a marketplace's platform account can carry a large share of all debits at peak.

hints: A check-then-debit is a read-modify-write. It needs one serialisation point per account, or a way to split the balance so that each part has one.
Credits commute and can be applied late; debits do not. Treat them differently during a partition.
With {{regions}} regions, ask what a majority is, and whether a majority survives losing one region.
followups: Walk through one debit end to end: request with idempotency key, check, ledger write, balance update, response. Where can it fail, and what does the client see each time?
The region that is home to 30% of accounts is lost for {{outage}}. What happens to their debits, credits and balance reads?
How would you let a hot account keep accepting debits in every region during a partition, with a provable cap on overdraft?
How do you show, every day, that each served balance equals the sum of its ledger entries, without stopping writes?
Finance asks for the balance of every account as of midnight UTC, consistent across all accounts. How do you produce it?

rules.ask: Region A approves a debit, then fails before replicating it. Region B approves another debit on the same balance. What prevents the overdraft?
Your coordinator's region is the one that just went down. What state are the in-flight debits in, and who resolves them?
With {{regions}} regions, how many must answer to commit, and what happens when one is lost?
The overdraft check reads a replica 2 seconds behind. Show a sequence of requests that overdraws the account.
One marketplace account takes a fifth of all debits. What throughput does one lock give you, and what do you do about it?

incidents: One of the {{regions}} regions is unreachable for {{outage}}. Accounts whose home is that region keep receiving payout and refund requests, which now arrive elsewhere.
During the failover, clients retry debits. After recovery you find a small number of debits applied twice, each pair with the same idempotency key, one in each region.
A nightly invariant check finds 37 accounts whose served available balance differs from the sum of their ledger entries.
One marketplace account takes a fifth of all debits at peak, and every one of them contends on the same balance record.

templates.title: Customers double-charged after a retry bug

cause: a client retry path that generated a new idempotency key on every attempt
a queue consumer that re-processed charge requests after a timeout
a deploy that skipped the idempotency check on one code path

sections.scenario: Your team owns a service that creates charges on behalf of merchants. For {{hours}} hours, {{cause}} caused about {{customers}} end customers to be charged twice for one purchase. Merchants are opening support tickets, some cardholders have already called their banks, and the second charges are beginning to settle. You are the most senior engineer on the team and the incident is yours to lead.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead the response: the first hour, the first day and the following weeks. Cover stopping the harm, identifying exactly who was affected, making customers whole, communicating with merchants and internal teams, and preventing a repeat. Then tell me about a real incident you led where customers lost money or trust (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You cannot delete or edit charges; corrections are new transactions (refunds or reversals). Merchants own the relationship with their customers. Some duplicates may already be disputed.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Contains first (feature flag, revert, server-side dedup guard); precise definition of a duplicate with a measured error rate; refunds through new transactions, coordinated with dispute handling; clear decision rights with legal, support and merchants; timely, factual communication; prevention at the right layer (server-side idempotency, invariants on charges per order) with an owner; real example has measurable evidence and a personal contribution, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the bug still live?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet when you are paged; the alert is a spike in charges per order.

clarifications.q: Can we refund on the merchants' behalf?
clarifications.a: Technically yes, but legal and support want a decision on consent and messaging first.

clarifications.q: How do we know which charges are duplicates?
clarifications.a: That is part of your job. Some customers genuinely bought twice.

clarifications.q: Who talks to merchants?
clarifications.a: Support and account teams, with your facts.

hints: Stop the bleeding before you diagnose: what is the fastest safe switch?
Define "duplicate" precisely and estimate your false positives before refunding anyone.
Refunding duplicates quickly also avoids disputes, which cost merchants fees and time.
followups: Your query finds 9% more suspected duplicates than the support tickets suggest. Do you refund all of them? Who decides?
A large merchant asks you not to refund automatically because they want to contact customers first. How do you handle different merchant preferences at scale?
Some duplicates are already disputed. What happens if you refund those too, and how do you avoid paying twice?
What did you change so the next idempotency failure is caught in minutes? Name the signal, threshold and owner.
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: The bug is in a client library merchants have already deployed. What can you roll back, and what can you not?
Some of those customers really did buy twice. How many would you refund wrongly, and what does that cost the merchant?
Name one change from the review that actually shipped, and how you verified it worked.
What did you personally decide or do?
How do you keep the review blameless when one engineer's change caused it?

templates.title: Rewrite the ledger service, or evolve it?

driver: volume expected to grow tenfold in two years
a new multi-currency product the current schema cannot represent
audit findings that some entries can be edited after posting

sections.scenario: The ledger service is {{age}} years old. It records every movement of money as entries, and dozens of services and finance reports depend on it. It caused {{incidents}} incidents last quarter. The trigger for the current debate is {{driver}}. Half of your {{team}}-person team wants a rewrite on a new design; the other half wants to evolve the current service. Leadership asks you for a recommendation within two weeks.
sections.problem: How would you reach and present the decision? Cover the evidence you gather, the options you compare (including hybrids), how you de-risk whichever path you choose, how you keep money correct during any migration, and how you bring both halves of the team along. Then describe a real architecture decision of similar weight that you led or strongly influenced, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The ledger cannot stop. Historical entries must remain queryable and auditable. Finance closes every month and cannot absorb a broken close.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence before opinion (incident causes, change lead time, limits that are structural vs neglected); options compared on explicit criteria including risk to money and cost of delay; a reversible, staged plan with parallel run and entry-level reconciliation; history and audit handled deliberately; team alignment through a written decision; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is there a deadline from the business?
clarifications.a: The trigger for the debate sets one; you should establish how firm it is.

clarifications.q: Can the team grow?
clarifications.a: Modestly; assume most of the work is done by today's team.

clarifications.q: Who must approve?
clarifications.a: Engineering leadership, with finance and the audit owner consulted.

clarifications.q: Are the incidents in one area?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet; that is part of the evidence.

hints: Separate the problems: which ones the current design cannot solve, and which ones are just neglected.
Any migration of a ledger needs a period where old and new run side by side and are reconciled entry by entry.
Write the decision down with the criteria and the reversal points, so the half that lost can see why.
followups: What would you have to see in the evidence to recommend a rewrite? And to recommend against one?
Describe the migration: dual writes, shadow reads or something else. How do you know the new system is right before it becomes the source of truth?
Three months in, the chosen path is behind schedule and the other camp says "told you so". What do you do?
How do you migrate {{age}} years of history, or do you?
In your real example, what evidence changed your mind, and what would you decide differently now?

rules.ask: During the rewrite the old service still needs fixes, and the pressure that started this debate does not wait. Who does that work?
Which seam do you cut first, and how do you prove that slice is correct before moving the next?
The two writes succeed in one system and fail in the other. Which one is the truth, and how do you repair the other?
Where did you personally disagree with the outcome, and what did you do about it?

templates.title: Warehouse spend for merchant reporting tripled

sections.scenario: Merchant reporting (downloadable reports, scheduled exports and the analytics behind dashboards) runs on a cloud data warehouse. Over {{weeks}} weeks its spend went from {{spend}}, while the number of active merchants grew {{growth}}. Finance wants a plan, and the reporting product team is worried that cuts will slow reports merchants rely on for their own month-end.
sections.problem: How would you lead the response? Cover how you find where the money goes, what you change first and what later, how you protect merchant-facing service levels and the correctness of financial reports, and how you keep spend from drifting again. Then tell me about a real time you reduced a significant cost (STAR, with numbers), or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Reports that merchants reconcile against payouts must stay exact. No merchant-visible report may get slower than its stated service level without the product team's agreement.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Normalises cost to growth; attributes spend to workloads and owners; finds root causes (full recomputes, over-refreshing, unpruned scans, idle compute) with evidence; sequences reversible quick wins and structural fixes; protects exactness and service levels; installs guardrails with owners; communicates trade-offs to finance and product; real example is measured and personal, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do we know which workloads cost what?
clarifications.a: Only partly; queries are not consistently tagged.

clarifications.q: Did anything launch recently?
clarifications.a: A scheduled export feature and a dashboard redesign shipped in the period.

clarifications.q: Is there a target?
clarifications.a: Finance asked for a credible plan, not a number. You may propose one.

clarifications.q: Who owns the warehouse?
clarifications.a: A platform team operates it; several teams run workloads on it.

hints: Normalise before you react: cost per merchant or per million payments tells you whether this is growth or waste.
Attribute spend to workloads and owners first; the top handful of queries usually explain most of it.
Separate quick reversible fixes from structural changes, and measure each.
followups: You find the new scheduled export recomputes each merchant's full history every night. What do you change, and how do you prove the exports are still exact?
A dashboard refreshes every minute for every open browser tab. The product team says freshness is the feature. How do you resolve it?
Which guardrails would stop this happening again: budgets, alerts, per-team attribution, review of new workloads? Who owns each?
How would you present the plan to finance and to the product team, who want different things?
In your real example, what was the saving, how was it measured, and what did it cost in other terms?

rules.ask: Spend already tripled. How does more compute reduce the bill?
Late refunds and disputes change past days. How does your incremental model stay exact?
What invalidates the cache when a late change arrives for a past day?
Which merchants notice, and who agreed?

templates.title: Real-time balances or audited end-of-day numbers?

sections.scenario: Product wants the merchant dashboard to show balances in real time, because {{audience}} keep asking how much they have right now. Finance wants the dashboard to show only audited end-of-day numbers, because intraday figures typically differ from the final ones by about {{gap}} and every difference becomes a support ticket or a question in an audit. Both teams have asked you, as the data lead, to back them. The roadmap needs an answer within {{deadline}}.
sections.problem: How would you handle the disagreement and reach a decision? Cover how you understand what each side actually needs, what options you put on the table, how the data would have to work for each, who decides and how, and how you would make the decision stick. Then describe a real disagreement between two teams that you helped resolve, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own the decision alone. Whatever ships must not show two different numbers for the same thing without explaining why.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Surfaces underlying needs; quantifies the intraday-to-final gap and its causes; proposes options with data implications (one ledger source, provisional vs final states, as-of labels, reconciliation of the two); clear decision rights and a fair escalation; disagree-and-commit when overruled; real example with a durable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Why do intraday and final numbers differ?
clarifications.a: Late refunds and disputes, fees finalised at settlement, and currency conversion. You should confirm the mix.

clarifications.q: Is there a regulatory requirement?
clarifications.a: Not for the dashboard specifically, but finance's audited reports are the official figures.

clarifications.q: Who is the final decider?
clarifications.a: The product director and the finance controller jointly; escalation goes to their common leader.

clarifications.q: Do merchants act on these numbers?
clarifications.a: Yes. Some decide on spending or payouts from them.

hints: Ask what decision each side is trying to protect; positions hide needs.
"Real-time" and "audited" can both be shown if they are clearly different things with clear labels and a known relationship.
Bring numbers: how often and how much do intraday figures move, and why.
followups: What would the dashboard show under your proposal, word for word, for a balance that may still change?
Finance agrees, but only if intraday numbers are never more than a stated amount away from the final ones. How do you measure that and what happens when it is exceeded?
The decision goes against your recommendation. What do you do next?
In your real example, how did you separate positions from needs, and how did you know the resolution held?

rules.ask: Which part of each side's need does your compromise give up, and did they agree to give it up?
What would you put in front of the decider, and how do you keep it fair to the side you disagree with?
How do you know merchants read and understand the label? What would you measure?
What is the source of the real-time number, and how does it converge to the audited one?

templates.title: Reconciliation scripts only one person understands

situation: is going on leave in six weeks
has given notice and leaves in a month
is paged at every month-end close and is burning out

sections.scenario: Month-end close depends on {{scripts}} reconciliation scripts that match the ledger against processor and bank files and produce the adjustments finance books. They run partly by hand, from one engineer's laptop and a shared server. One engineer wrote most of them and is the only person who understands them, and that engineer {{situation}}. Finance must close within {{close_days}} business days.
sections.problem: What do you do, in what order, and how do you get the time for it? Cover the immediate risk to the next close, how you transfer knowledge, how you make the scripts safe to change, whether and when you replace them, and how you treat the engineer. Then tell me about a real piece of risky technical debt you reduced, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The next close must not slip. Feature work for the quarter is already committed. Finance must be able to explain every adjustment to auditors.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Sequences risk: next close first (inventory, version control, runbook, shadow run by another engineer), then tests from historical outputs, then hardening and scheduling, then optional replacement with parallel run; treats the engineer with respect and recognition; makes the business case in concrete terms and secures time; keeps adjustments explainable; real example with measured risk reduction and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the scripts in version control?
clarifications.a: Some are; others exist only on the shared server.

clarifications.q: Are there tests?
clarifications.a: No. There are past close outputs, kept by finance.

clarifications.q: Is the engineer willing to help?
clarifications.a: Yes, but their time is limited.

clarifications.q: Can you rewrite them in the new data platform?
clarifications.a: Eventually, perhaps. Not before the next close.

hints: First make the next close survivable without that person: inventory, runbook, and a shadow run by someone else.
Past close outputs are your test oracle: rerun old inputs and compare with what finance booked.
Make the case for time in terms the business feels: a late close, an audit finding, one person's health.
followups: Show me the first two weeks: what exists at the end of week one, and at the end of week two?
A shadow rerun of last month's close differs from what was booked by a few hundred minor units on one source. What do you do?
Your manager says the roadmap cannot give up any time. How do you make the case, and what do you do if the answer is still no?
When would you replace the scripts rather than harden them, and how would you run old and new in parallel?
In your real example, how did you measure that the risk was actually lower?

rules.ask: The next close is in three weeks. What exactly runs that close, and who runs it?
How do you know the runbook works? Who has followed it without help?
How do you recognise that person's contribution while removing the dependency on them?
Which inputs and outputs do you use as the oracle, and how do you know they were right?
